article.headline: The Greeks Are Coming for Retail: How Dealer-Positioning Data Became the Quant's New Edge
article.lede: For decades, the proprietary risk sheets of options market makers were as inaccessible to ordinary traders as the Federal Reserve's trading desk. A new generation of data vendors — fed by CBOE-licensed feeds and delivered by API — is changing that arithmetic, one gamma surface at a time.
article.body:
The chart that @quantedOptions posted on April 16, 2026 would have looked like alien scripture to most traders a decade ago: a colour-coded grid of dollar figures arrayed across strike prices from 5,950 to 7,090 on the S&P 500 index, labelled with three exotic Greek letters and denominated in numbers that ranged from a few hundred million to negative two billion dollars. It is, in fact, a dealer positioning map — an attempt to reconstruct, from publicly observable options open interest, exactly how much hedging pressure Wall Street's market-making desks will exert on the underlying market as prices, volatility, and time all move simultaneously. That such a thing now exists in a widget deliverable at one-minute resolution to anyone with a Python environment and a free-trial API key is a genuine structural shift in who gets to see the market's wiring.

The three exposures on display each describe a different channel through which dealers transmit force into the equity market. Gamma exposure — GEX, in the shorthand — is the most widely discussed: it measures the aggregate change in a dealer's total delta (their net directional exposure) for every one-point move in the S&P 500. When dealers are net long gamma, as they typically are after selling options to hedgers and retail buyers, they must sell index futures when prices rise and buy them when prices fall — a dampening, mean-reverting influence on intraday moves. Flip the sign, as happens around major strike expirations or in vol spikes, and dealers become net short gamma: they must buy strength and sell weakness, amplifying rather than containing directional moves. The large negative GEX readings visible at certain strikes on the QuantData chart — that minus $2.0 billion figure — mark zones where a sustained breach could mechanically trigger dealer selling.

Vanna introduces a second dimension: it measures how much a dealer's delta changes as implied volatility shifts, rather than as the underlying price moves. In practice, this means that a broad calm — a compression of the VIX, say, after a patch of turbulence — forces market makers to buy back the futures they had used to hedge, even if the S&P 500 itself sits perfectly still. The buy-pressure arrives not because equities are rising but because fear is receding. SpotGamma has documented this dynamic as the architecture of the "volatility-reset rally," those peculiar up-days in low-volume conditions that confound fundamental analysts looking for a catalyst. The effect is real, though its magnitude is disputed: estimating dealer vanna exposure requires knowing how much of the open interest is held by natural sellers of volatility versus natural buyers, a decomposition that no public data source can resolve with certainty.

Charm — the third exposure — is subtler still: it tracks the time decay of delta itself. Even if both price and volatility remain frozen, an option's probability of finishing in-the-money drifts continuously toward zero or one as expiration approaches, dragging the dealer's hedge along with it. In a market where zero-days-to-expiration contracts — 0DTE options, those that expire on the day they are traded — now account for more than sixty percent of all SPX option volume by contract count, charm operates on a compressed timescale. A position that would have drifted gently over a week now snaps to its terminal state within hours; dealers must rebalance intraday with an urgency that has no historical precedent. The result, observed by researchers at CBOE and in peer-reviewed work surveying the 2024-2025 period, is a tendency for SPX to "pin" near high-open-interest strikes in the final two hours of the session, as dealer charm hedging converges on the same levels from multiple expiry ladders simultaneously.

The commercial ecosystem packaging this data for retail quants has grown rapidly alongside the underlying flows. SpotGamma, which pioneered the dealer-GEX frame for mass audiences around 2020, now integrates its data into Bloomberg Terminal. Rivals including MenthorQ, QuantData, FlashAlpha, and vol.land have followed with their own dashboard and API offerings, each advertising CBOE-licensed data as a credential that distinguishes professional feeds from models that simply back-calculate Greeks from closing open interest. The distinction matters: intraday feed latency, the treatment of customer-side versus market-maker-side positioning, and the decomposition of end-of-day versus opening prints all affect the signal meaningfully. The 1-minute cadence that QuantData's advertisement highlights is a selling point precisely because 0DTE gamma can flip sign multiple times during a single session as new series open and old ones expire.

The limitations of these tools deserve as much attention as the mechanics. GEX and its relatives are estimates of a distribution of positions, not verified balance-sheet data; the assumption that all short options are held by dealers who must delta-hedge continuously is a simplification that academic work has consistently found to be imprecise. CBOE's own research argues that net dealer gamma hedging from 0DTE flows represents at most a fraction of a percent of daily SPX liquidity — a finding that sits uncomfortably alongside the narratives built on GEX. More fundamentally, these surfaces tell you the structural landscape of hedging pressure, not the path the market will actually take through it: a large negative-GEX strike is a gravitational attractor only if price approaches it, and nothing in the dealer-positioning framework predicts whether that approach will occur. Used as a map of conditional leverage rather than a directional signal, the data is genuinely useful. Used as a timing system, it has a long history of being confidently wrong.

concepts.definition: The estimated aggregate change in options market makers' total directional position (delta) for a one-point move in the underlying index, derived from observable open interest; positive GEX implies dealers will buy dips and sell rallies (dampening volatility), negative GEX implies they will amplify moves.

A second-order options Greek measuring how much a dealer's delta — and therefore their hedging position — changes when implied volatility shifts, independent of any move in the underlying price; falling volatility under net short-vanna dealer positioning mechanically forces dealers to buy futures.

Also called delta decay: the rate at which an option's delta changes purely as time passes toward expiration, even if price and volatility are unchanged; as expiry approaches, charm accelerates, compelling dealers to rebalance hedges intraday rather than overnight.

Zero-days-to-expiration options — contracts that are opened and expire on the same calendar day; they now represent over 60% of SPX option volume by contract count and concentrate extreme gamma and charm exposure into intraday timeframes.

The reconstructed aggregate Greek exposures (gamma, vanna, charm, delta) held by options market makers, estimated from public open-interest data under the assumption that dealers are net sellers of options who continuously delta-hedge; used to infer where systematic hedging flows will pressure the underlying market.

article.fact_check: 0DTE share of SPX volume >60% confirmed by CBOE State of the Options Industry 2025 and MenthorQ guide. Total industry options volume of 15.2 billion contracts in 2025 (+26% YoY) per CBOE. CBOE research finding that net market maker gamma hedging from 0DTE is 'at best 0.2% of SPX daily liquidity' per cboe.com Volatility Insights. SpotGamma's Bloomberg Terminal integration confirmed on spotgamma.com. The QuantData / quantdata.us brand is corroborated by their help-center article on GEX methodology.
article.thread_summary: Single promotional post by @quantedOptions advertising a CBOE-licensed market-maker data API offering GEX, vanna, and charm surfaces at 1-minute cadence for SPX, illustrated by a multi-Greek 'Gamma Surface' chart timestamped April 16 2026 12:02 ET, with strike coverage from 5,950 to 7,090 and a secondary SPX GEX + price panel.

ticker_spy.name: SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust
ticker_spy.blurb: The oldest and largest U.S. equity exchange-traded fund, launched in January 1993 by State Street Global Advisors as a vehicle to track the S&P 500 Index — a market-capitalisation-weighted benchmark of 500 large U.S. companies maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices. SPY holds all constituent stocks in proportion to their index weight, with Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Amazon and Meta typically constituting the top five positions. It trades continuously during market hours with daily volume in the hundreds of millions of shares, making it the world's most liquid single-listed equity security by dollar volume. Expense ratio: 0.0945% annually. SPY is often used as a proxy for 'the market' in both retail portfolios and institutional hedging strategies.
ticker_spy.recent: The S&P 500 closed at approximately 7,230 on May 1, 2026, representing a YTD gain of roughly 5.1% for 2026. The index's Shiller CAPE ratio stood near 40.9 as of early May 2026 — among the two highest readings in recorded history and exceeded only briefly during the 1999-2000 dot-com peak. The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.5–3.75% at its April 2026 meeting, maintaining a pause in the cutting cycle that began in late 2024.

poster_quantedoptions.blurb: QuantedOptions is the X/Twitter presence for QuantData, a market-data vendor that distributes CBOE-licensed options analytics — including dealer gamma exposure (GEX), vanna, and charm surfaces — via REST API at intraday (one-minute) cadence. The account targets quantitative developers, systematic traders, and retail options traders under the tagline 'quant, vibe coder, Python trader.' Its product is in the same commercial category as SpotGamma, MenthorQ, and Tier1Alpha: structured dealer-positioning data sold as an analytical layer on top of public CBOE open-interest and quote feeds.
poster_quantedoptions.credibility_note: QuantData advertises its data as CBOE-licensed, which implies a direct data-distribution agreement rather than self-calculated Greeks from free end-of-day files — a meaningful but unauditable distinction from the outside. The company's exact founding date and team composition are not publicly disclosed. Free-trial API access was available as of April 2026. The account's engagement pattern (promotional charts, data samples, API pitch) is consistent with a data-vendor marketing account rather than original research. Treat product claims about data quality and latency as unverified marketing.
